articles.desc: Trait-based approaches have revolutionized ecology by enabling the characterization of biodiversity through species’ ecological strategies. articles.title: Linking Population Genomics and Movement Ecology for Shark Conservation
articles.desc: Climate change and overexploitation are increasingly threatening sharks, with pelagic species among the most affected. The complex ecology and life histories of these species, however, pose major challenges for conservation planning. Here, we examine how integrating genomics and movement ecology can better inform the conservation of highly migratory sharks. The growing availability of reference genomes and expanding population genomic datasets in sharks, coupled with advances in biologging, creates unprecedented opportunities to integrate these approaches and link long-term, population-level evolutionary processes with short-term individual, behavioural patterns. This mini review explores research applications that integrate both fields to overcome their individual limitations and strengthen the evidence and conclusions used to inform conservation. Then we discuss, based on previous studies, how this framework can address specific conservation objectives and lead to decision-ready outcomes, including the delineation of management units, the design of spatial and stock-specific fisheries management measures, and the assessment of species' vulnerability to climate change. We conclude by highlighting that the translation of this knowledge into practice requires engagement with the scientific and management bodies responsible for evaluating the evidence, advising decision-makers, and implementing shark conservation measures.

articles.title: Duality of root‐dominated net soil organic carbon gain and mycelium‐mediated carbon loss in hyper‐arid afforestation
articles.desc: Summary Afforestation regulates soil organic carbon (SOC) sequestration via plant‐ and microbial‐derived carbon (C) inputs, but root‐ and mycelium‐derived C inputs differ in quantity, turnover, and stabilization mechanisms, and these differences may shift as stands develop. However, how root vs mycelium pathways drive SOC dynamics across a dryland afforestation chronosequence remains unclear. Using the ingrowth‐core method along a dryland afforestation chronosequence (young forests, middle‐aged forests, and mature forests), we quantified the contributions of root and mycelium pathways to SOC. The root pathway promoted SOC accumulation via particulate organic C and mineral‐associated organic C inputs, contributing to 77.19–85.05% of the SOC changes. By contrast, the mycelium pathway induced net SOC loss via particulate organic C depletion, contributing to 14.95–22.81% of the SOC changes. SOC concentrations peaked in middle‐aged forests, whereas relative SOC stability peaked in young forests. This study provides the first quantitative assessment of the distinct contributions of root and mycelium pathways to SOC accumulation and stabilization during dryland afforestation, advancing understanding of their roles in regulating SOC dynamics. As climate change intensifies land‐use pressure, management strategies should integrate stage‐specific root and mycelial traits to enhance SOC sequestration in arid forests.

Yet spatial prioritization frameworks rarely integrate land-use resistance and climate stability into a unified approach, limiting their operational value for landscape management and policy. Objectives We aimed to develop an ecological connectivity framework that jointly incorporates land-use resistance and climate stability to map linkages among protected areas, and to quantify and communicate methodological uncertainty arising from key parameterization choices. Methods We applied the framework to Portugal's terrestrial protected-area network. Using a full factorial design, we varied land-use resistance, climate resistance, and dispersal capacity across multiple weightings to generate optimized linkage solutions. Selection-frequency maps derived from these solutions fed a second optimization round, producing an ensemble connectivity solution and buffered corridors. Results Individual solutions covered 0.74% of Portugal's unprotected land; the ensemble covered 0.07%, rising to 2.3% after a 1 km buffer. Dispersal capacity parameterization introduced greater uncertainty in connectivity outcomes than land-use or climate resistance scores, suggesting it deserves particular attention in future studies. articles.title: Newly planted woodlands improve connectivity for woodland fauna, flora and fungi
articles.desc: Context Young planted woodlands may only support a small proportion of the biodiversity found in mature woodlands but may play an important role in promoting species movements and enhancing biodiversity due to their emerging structural similarities. Objectives We assessed whether recently planted woodlands increase connectivity between mature woodland patches relative to agricultural fields, and whether responses vary across active (small mammals, ground invertebrates) and passive (plants, fungi) dispersers. Methods We used a multi-taxa natural experiment across paired sites where mature woodlands were either connected by planted woodland or separated by farmland. Movement was quantified using PIT-tagging of small mammals and beetles, pitfall trapping, vegetation surveys, airborne spore traps and soil eDNA metabarcoding. A Bayesian beta-binomial model estimated taxon-specific habitat preferences for dispersal. Results Although we did not detect inter-patch movements, we detected higher movement of wood mice, ground active invertebrates, plants, and fungi into new woodlands relative to agricultural fields, whereas, field voles exhibited minimal movement, and some airborne fungal groups showed reduced movement within planted woodlands. Young woodlands generally supported higher woodland specialist richness, abundance or occurrence than fields but did not support the full complement of species associated with mature woodlands. articles.title: Riparian vegetation connectivity and composition jointly shape larval aquatic insect diversity across local and regional scales
articles.desc: Context Riparian vegetation is a major driver of freshwater biodiversity; however, the structural degradation of riparian vegetation due to anthropogenic pressures poses a major threat to riverine ecosystems worldwide. Objectives This study examined how riparian vegetation connectivity and composition jointly shape aquatic insect communities. We specifically asked whether connectivity and forest type have distinct effects on local and regional diversity. Methods We conducted field surveys of Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera, and Trichoptera (EPT) at 198 sites across the Yangtze River Basin. Sites were classified by riparian connectivity degree, and deciduous and natural forest cover were quantified using high-resolution remote sensing data. Results Our results revealed that increased vegetation connectivity enhanced α-diversity by promoting adult dispersal and the stability of larval habitats. By contrast, β-diversity showed a nonlinear response to increases in vegetation connectivity; specifically, it declined initially due to community homogenization and then increased because of species turnover. Higher deciduous forest cover was associated with increased α-diversity under medium and high connectivity; however, its effects on β-diversity were variable. Natural forests consistently promoted both α- and β-diversity, especially under high connectivity, and this was associated with the complex structure and heterogeneous habitat distribution of natural forests. articles.desc: Agricultural expansion and landscape fragmentation are altering ecological connectivity in agro-pastoral transition zones. Ecological security patterns can support landscape conservation and restoration, but their reliability is constrained by uncertainty in ecological source identification and resistance surface construction. This study identified suitable methods for constructing ecological security patterns in ecologically fragile agricultural landscapes. We compared three ecological source identification approaches and five machine learning models for resistance surface construction, and assessed their implications for ecological network optimization in western Jilin, China. We assessed five ecosystem services and compared ordered weighted averaging, morphological spatial pattern analysis, and ecosystem service significance assessment for ecological source identification. We compared five machine learning models to construct the ecological resistance surface. Based on the selected sources and resistance surface, we used minimum cumulative resistance and circuit theory to identify corridors, pinch points, and barriers. Ecosystem services showed spatial heterogeneity, with most services decreasing from east to west. articles.title: Regional tree migration outpaces local migration due to fragmentation and life history traits
articles.desc: Predictions of tree species range shifts have emphasized regional migration rates, while how local migration drives regional migration remains poorly understood. Landscape fragmentation is a major source of migration lag, but its interactions with species life history traits remain understudied. We aimed to clarify mechanisms underlying differences between local and regional migration rates, quantify how fragmentation and life history traits jointly shape migration, and assess temporal variation in these effects. We quantified local and regional migration rates of temperate tree species with contrasting life history traits across fragmented landscapes. LANDIS PRO incorporated key demographic processes, including seed dispersal, colonization, establishment, growth, and mortality. We assessed direct and interactive effects of fragmentation over short (0–30 years), medium (30–65 years), and long (65–100 years) timescales. Regional migration was nearly five times faster than local migration, and increasing fragmentation reduced regional migration and increased migration lags. Fragmentation more strongly constrained regional migration, whereas, among the six focal species, life history traits such as maturity age and seed production showed stronger associations with local migration. articles.desc: Climate change and anthropogenic stressors are degrading coastal biogenic habitats, disrupting the vital pathways fish use to shift from nearshore nurseries to offshore reef environments. Although fishes are critical for ecosystem health, spatial management rarely accounts for the interconnectedness of fish habitat needs across their life cycle. To examine and compare drivers of habitat use for subadult size classes of five habitat-shifting fishes from two feeding guilds: mesopredators and herbivores. To assess the multi-species suitability of existing management zones. We used MaxEnt to model habitat suitability for our focal fishes across the Florida Keys, USA, and performed permutation analyses to compare habitat use patterns and drivers among species. We used predicted suitability maps to quantify suitability for 58 management zones. Benthic habitat type was the strongest driver, with patch- and aggregate-reefs emerging as the most suitable across species. Habitats were more moderately suitable for mesopredators across the nearshore-offshore gradient, while S. guacamaia stood out among the herbivores as preferring nearshore and mid-channel habitats over offshore habitats. articles.title: Legacy effects of land use land cover change on species distribution dynamics: evidence from a landscape of diverse biogeographic crossroads
articles.desc: Context Land use and land cover (LULC) change is a key driver of biodiversity distribution, yet species responses vary among taxa, habitats, and regions. Because species responses are context-dependent, understanding how ecological characteristics and landscape history influence biodiversity distribution is essential for conservation planning. Objectives We evaluated how nearly two centuries of LULC change have influenced vertebrate distribution dynamics across Texas, USA, a landscape of biogeographic crossroads. We tested whether habitat specialization, taxonomic identity, conservation status, and ecoregional context better explain range expansion, contraction, and redistribution than landscape change metrics alone. Methods We compared historical and contemporary distributions of 100 native vertebrate species (mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians). Multi-temporal LULC datasets (1850–2023) were integrated with species occurrences, habitat associations, and ecoregional data to identify drivers of distribution range change. Results LULC change was spatially heterogeneous, driven by agricultural expansion, cropland abandonment, shrubland encroachment, and urbanization. Most species shifted ranges, with responses varying by habitat, taxon, and ecoregion. articles.title: Spatial distribution and environmental drivers of wild honey bee nesting patterns in the Eastern Cape Province, South Africa
articles.desc: Spatial clusters of animal nests can be driven by mating behaviors, social benefits, and landscape heterogeneity. Unmanaged honey bees (Hymenoptera: Apidae: Apis spp.) have been documented nesting in clustered spatial distributions. However, environmental features influencing unmanaged honey bee nesting patterns have been largely understudied, especially for wild honey bees ( A. mellifera ) across Africa. We worked in the Eastern Cape Province, South Africa to characterize the spatial distribution and environmental drivers of wild honey bee nesting patterns. We surveyed 1 km 2 grid cells for wild honey bee nests using beelining techniques, with which we followed foragers from stands with sugar water to their nest entrances. We used nest locality data to test for complete spatial randomness using Monte Carlo simulations with mean nearest-neighbor distances. We used generalized linear mixed-effects models and a model selection approach to explore impacts of 11 land management, vegetation, and terrain covariates on patterns of nest density (nests/0.25 km 2 ). We located 97 occupied nests within 16 km 2 across five field sites. Wild honey bee colonies nested in both clustered and random spatial patterns. articles.title: Impacts of needle-leaved forests landscape pattern and environmental factors on the spatial differentiation of pine wilt disease in China
articles.desc: Following its emergence in China, pine wilt disease (PWD) has continuously expanded, creating substantial risks to regional forest ecosystems. However, most existing research emphasizes climate and other macro-scale associated factors, and lacks long-term and systematic analysis approached through the lens of forest landscape patterns. The research focuses on describing the spatiotemporal dynamics of PWD in China across the period 1982–2020 and identifying the dominant factors influencing its distribution. We specifically examined how needle-leaved forest landscape patterns interact with environmental conditions to shape the spread of PWD across regions. We applied the optimal parameters-based geographical detector (OPGD) model to analyze the spatial differentiation of PWD outbreaks. Needle-leaved forest landscape metrics and environmental variables were integrated to evaluate their individual and combined effects on disease spread. PWD has progressively expanded over the past four decades. The epidemic was primarily distributed along the southeastern coastal zones and subsequently extended toward the northwestern interior. articles.desc: Context Investigating how habitat specialists express population-level differences in habitat preferences and movement behaviour across contrasting landscapes and abiotic environments allows us to distinguish patterns that are consistent across populations from those that are population-specific responses to local conditions. Objectives We examined space use, hunting habitat selection and diel activity between Eurasian Pygmy Owl ( Glaucidium passerinum ) populations occupying boreal (south-west Finland) and subalpine (Western Italian Alps) forests, to assess the consistency of these patterns across regions with contrasting landscape structure and photoperiod. Methods From 2021 to 2024, we GPS-tagged 26 breeding males (13 per region), obtaining 6076 GPS locations. We estimated 90% home-range areas using autocorrelated kernel density estimators (AKDE). Hunting habitat selection was examined with resource selection functions implemented as GLMMs, and diel activity was characterised by modelling activity probability with cyclic GAMs. Results Pygmy owls behaved as clear forest specialists in both regions: 90% AKDE home ranges were dominated by continuous forest, with consistent avoidance of open habitats and recent clear-cuts. Activity was diurnal, with peaks at dawn and dusk. Boreal individuals showed extended activity periods associated with prolonged daylight and twilight. articles.desc: The impacts of non-native Emerald Ash Borer (EAB) are likely to be most severe in black ash wetlands, possibly requiring preemptive forest management to maintain ecosystem functions such as carbon storage. We used a silvicultural experiment in northern Minnesota to evaluate how EAB-induced mortality and preemptive management affect total ecosystem carbon storage and the distribution of carbon among ecosystem pools. Treatments included tree girdling to emulate EAB-induced tree mortality, clearcutting, 20% canopy removal with group selection and an undisturbed control. Ash trees ( Fraxinus spp.) in the control black ash wetlands stored 116.7 (± 5.3) Mg C ha −1 , and live tree carbon storage increased by 1.8 (± 0.12) Mg C ha −1 yr −1 over the study period. Twelve years after treatment, total ecosystem carbon was lower in all treatments relative to the control and lowest in clearcuts. In the emulated-EAB treatment, representing a do-nothing scenario, total ecosystem carbon decreased by 22% relative to the control, with 71.6 (± 4.7) Mg C ha −1 remaining in deadwood pools where continued decomposition will lead to further carbon storage loss. Understory carbon increased in clearcuts following treatment, but only a small fraction was associated with potential canopy-replacement species. articles.title: Drivers of Spatial Change in Seagrass Carbon Stock Amid Shifting Species Dominance
articles.desc: Seagrass meadows are recognized for their significant role in blue carbon sequestration and storage. However, these ecosystems are being altered by climate change, and consequently so too are the ecosystem services they provide. Here, we evaluate drivers of spatial variation in carbon storage among seagrass meadows in the Lower Chesapeake Bay, which underwent a temperature-driven shift in species dominance from Zostera marina to Ruppia maritima in the last decade. We collected 140 cores from meadows of varying historic vegetated cover, depth, and dominant species identity and measured belowground carbon stock, grain size, and associated meadow characteristics. We then used a structural equation model to develop a single causal network to evaluate the drivers of spatial variation in sediment carbon storage across seagrass meadows. We show that site and both seagrass species and characteristics influence carbon stocks, but surprisingly, meadow age did not have explanatory power. In the Chesapeake Bay, Ruppia meadows have less carbon storage potential compared to Zostera when at similar depths ( Ruppia : 25.0 mg C cm −2 , Zostera : 31.4 mg C cm −2 ). However, due to climate-driven temperature increases, Ruppia occupies more of the optimal near-shore “real estate” for carbon storage than it did historically. articles.title: Soil Microbial Community Patterns after a Large Forest Fire in Temperate Central Europe
articles.desc: Wildfires are a major ecological driver impacting terrestrial ecosystems, yet their belowground impacts remain poorly understood in Central European temperate forests. We investigated soil microbial responses during the first post-fire year following the large 2022 wildfire in the Bohemian and Saxon Switzerland National Parks (Czechia and Germany). We compared soil microbial communities across three forest types differing in fire sensitivity ( Fagus sylvatica , Pinus sylvestris, and Picea abies stands) and examined how forest type, aboveground burn severity, soil burn severity, and soil properties structured prokaryotic and fungal communities. Prokaryotic richness remained largely stable across burn severities, although the diversity of prokaryotes and gene copy numbers declined with soil burn severity. In contrast, fungal communities showed stronger responses. Fungal richness and diversity decreased with soil burn severity, while fungal gene copy numbers increased in stands of low aboveground severity. Microbial community composition shifted in response to fire, with pronounced turnover in fungal communities. Variation partitioning indicated that the composition was jointly influenced by forest type and aboveground burn severity, whereas soil properties explained little additional variation. articles.desc: Litterfall, a key ecosystem process linking vegetation dynamics, carbon flux, and nutrient cycling, can be substantially altered by disease. However, effects of disease on both its production and spatial distribution are not well understood. We examined the effects of a dieback disease on leaf litterfall in forests dominated by a susceptible foundation tree species Agathis australis (kauri). Using leaf litterfall data and mapped trees from stands of varying successional stages and disease severity, we parameterised a spatially explicit Bayesian inverse model to estimate species-specific leaf litter production and dispersal for eight focal species as functions of tree size, distance from trunk, and disease severity. Kauri tree-level litterfall initially increased with disease severity but declined sharply after severe canopy loss. Due to the dominance of kauri, stand-level litterfall production mirrored effects of the disease at kauri tree-level litterfall, across all successional stages. On average, healthy stands produced 129.2 g m −2 year −1 less than a stand undergoing branch dieback and 142.7 g m −2 year −1 more than a stand with severe canopy dieback. articles.title: Sociodemographic Factors and Land Use Shape Perceptions of Ecosystem Services in Reservoirs of Semiarid Regions
articles.desc: Community perceptions of ecosystem services are shaped by individuals’ local contexts and their direct interactions with the environment. Examining these relationships enables a better understanding of how human perceptions of ecosystem services are associated with anthropogenic environmental change. In this study, we assessed the relationship between ecosystem service perceptions in riverside communities of semiarid reservoirs and sociodemographic variables, as well as the extent to which different land uses and land covers influence these perceptions. Interviews were conducted with residents living along the margins of the Sumé, Poções, and Cordeiro reservoirs (Paraíba River Basin) and the Sabugí, Passagem das Traíras, and Cruzeta reservoirs (Piranhas-Açu River Basin) in Northeast Brazil. Overall, 84% of the ecosystem services perceived by respondents were provisioning services, 12% were cultural services, and only 4% were regulation and maintenance services. Nevertheless, reservoirs surrounded by larger forested areas presented higher proportions of perceived regulation and maintenance services, whereas those with greater human occupation showed higher proportions of perceived provisioning services. The perception of provision services was negatively correlated with forest cover and positively correlated with human occupation. These patterns indicate a gap in ecological awareness among riparian communities, potentially linked to anthropogenic pressures on these ecosystems.

articles.desc: Mountain pine ( Pinus mugo Turra) is a key high-elevation species in the European Alps. It primarily establishes on exposed, erosion-prone sites and supports large soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks by sequestering carbon, stabilising soils, and preventing erosion. These functions are increasingly threatened as global change-related pressures like invasive pathogens impact mountain pine health. We investigated how declining mountain pine health affects SOC in Berchtesgaden National Park (BGNP), Germany. We studied two alternative vegetation states as potential outcomes of mountain pine decline, conifer-dominated forest and sparsely vegetated unstocked areas, and compared them to healthy and ailing mountain pine stands. We found that a transition from mountain pine to forest would have little effect on SOC ( p = 0.055). However, a trajectory to unstocked areas (with no woody plants establishing after mountain pine die-off) could result in 47.3% lower SOC compared to healthy mountain pine ( p < 0.001). To better understand the temporal development and landscape-scale consequences of such a potential loss of woody vegetation on areas currently stocked by mountain pine, we combined field data with carbon cycle simulations. Reduction of redox-active organic matter (RAOM) is one understudied mechanism where microbes use solid-phase (i.e., peat) organic matter as a terminal electron acceptor in anaerobic respiration. RAOM reduction suppresses methanogenesis due to energetic favorability and is often considered as an explanation for why certain peatland ecosystems produce less CH 4 than expected after accounting for other electron acceptors. Given the role of RAOM in regulating CH 4 production, we compiled datasets from boreal peatlands in the USA that quantified RAOM redox state using an electron shuttling capacity (ESC) assay and evaluated how RAOM reduction predicted CH 4 production in laboratory and in situ field incubations. Although structural differences across riverine, fringe, basin, and scrub ecotypes (e.g., tree height, species diversity, basal area) have been quantified, there remains a knowledge gap regarding the extent of interactions among these factors at regional and local scales, and the net productivity of these systems, especially in scrub mangrove wetlands. articles.desc: Elephants were a major driver of tree stem mortality in Africa, but their impacts are now spatially constrained and they no longer topple trees across the continent. Thus, most African landscapes lack a key ecological agent that helped maintain diversity and functioning. Even ecologists living in Africa fail to anticipate the rampant destruction of trees that can occur when elephants live in and move through landscapes. If we can build in a consensus on the degree of above-ground tree turnover that is inherent in different contexts, it would inform restoration projects and ecological definitions of degradation. We collated empirical data on treefall in ecosystems with and without elephants and predicted past tree loss spatially. The metrics used (%trees or #trees ha −1 ) reveal assumptions about the processes controlling elephant damage. On average elephants knock down 5.4 [IQR 3.0–8.3] % of the trees in an ecosystem per annum. Mapping this into places that no longer contain elephants reveals the above-ground biomass turnover that would have been the norm for millennia before elephants were widely exterminated. On average, this is ~ 1/3 of woody biomass production but at a local scale it can often exceed production. There is an urgent need for better theory on elephant tree interactions, and restoration projects should embrace the rapid turnover dynamics these ecosystems evolved with.

articles.title: Season-Specific Effects of Marine Heatwaves on Macrofaunal Community Composition and Ecosystem Processes
articles.desc: Marine HeatWaves (MHWs) increasingly modify marine ecosystems, and this is most prominent when high extreme summer temperatures exceed species’ tolerances. Less is known about the effects on ecosystem structure and processes of relative extreme temperatures in other seasons, despite heatwaves being increasingly common throughout the year. We conducted four repetitive laboratory experiments, in winter, spring, summer and autumn, to investigate the effects of seasonal MHWs on the processes and structure of natural benthic communities. Intact sediment cores were exposed to climatologically normal and strong MHW temperatures for 15 days. Community respiration and nutrient fluxes were measured every 5 days, and the community composition and their vertical distribution in the sediment were assessed at the end of each experiment. Our results showed season-specific changes in community metabolism due to MHWs, with the strongest impact in summer, followed by autumn, spring and least in winter. Notably, no mortality-induced differences in the composition over the whole communities between control and MHW treatments were detected. In summer, a migration into deeper sediments was observed, with the fauna possibly seeking a thermal refuge, highlighting a response to high absolute temperatures. Soil health and One Health implications in the anthropocene: a perspective on microbiome engineering
articles.desc: Background Climate change and Anthropocene pressures accelerate soil degradation, threatening agricultural productivity, ecosystems, and human health. Within the One Health framework, soils are critical living systems. However, while physical and chemical dimensions of soil health are well studied, the biological dimension—particularly microbiome functional diversity—remains heavily underutilized in climate-resilient agriculture. Rationale We argue that microbiome functional diversity is the missing biological foundation linking Soil Health and One Health. Rather than viewing microbiomes as isolated components, we propose they be treated as interconnected functional networks regulating resilience across soil, plant, animal, and human systems. We position microbiome engineering as a strategic research priority to translate ecological knowledge into sustainable agricultural solutions. Methods Here, it was demonstrated that synthetic bacterial consortia ( Bacillus velezensis YY13, B . subtilis JN1, and Pseudomonas chlororaphis JN72) colonizing tomato roots confer resistance against Fusarium wilt. articles.desc: Background and aims Soil acidity and aluminium toxicity cause significant yield losses in wheat. articles.desc: Heatwaves are increasing in intensity, frequency, and duration and may drive the responses of organisms to climate change more strongly than gradual increases in mean temperature.
